data.q: What is the primary purpose of a test spy in JavaScript testing?
o: To replace a function with a fake implementation
To record information about function calls without changing behavior
data.e: A spy wraps a function to track calls, arguments, return values, and exceptions while preserving the original behavior.

data.q: In Jest, which method creates a mock function that can track calls and optionally replace implementation?
data.e: jest.fn() creates a new mock function. jest.spyOn() spies on an existing object method.

data.q: When using Sinon.js, what is the difference between a stub and a spy?
o: A stub replaces behavior; a spy only observes
A spy replaces behavior; a stub only observes
A stub is for async only; a spy is for sync only
data.e: A stub replaces the target function's behavior with a custom one, while a spy wraps the original to record calls without altering it.

data.q: How do you restore a spy created with sinon.spy() or jest.spyOn() after a test?
data.e: Both Sinon and Jest spies provide a .restore() method to revert the original function. Call it in afterEach or cleanup.

data.q: Which Jest matcher checks if a mock function was called with specific arguments?
data.e: toHaveBeenCalledWith verifies the mock was called with the exact arguments provided.

Makes the stub throw an error
Makes the stub call the original function
data.e: resolves() is a convenience method to make a stub return a resolved Promise, useful for mocking async functions.

data.q: In Jest, how do you mock an entire module (e.g., axios) for a test file?
data.e: jest.mock('module-name') automatically mocks the module and its exports, allowing you to control behavior in tests.

data.q: What is a common use case for mocking the system clock (e.g., using sinon.useFakeTimers or jest.useFakeTimers)?
o: Testing code that uses setTimeout, setInterval, or Date.now
data.e: Fake timers allow deterministic control over time-dependent code, advancing time synchronously in tests.

data.q: When using jest.spyOn(object, 'method'), what happens if you don't call mockRestore()?
o: The spy persists across tests, potentially causing side effects
The original method is permanently deleted
Nothing; Jest cleans up automatically after each test
data.e: Jest does not automatically restore spies created with spyOn; you must call mockRestore() (or use jest.restoreAllMocks()) to avoid leaking mocks between tests.

data.q: Which of the following best describes a 'mock' in the context of unit testing?
o: A test double that replaces a real dependency with controllable behavior
A function that logs all calls to the console
A copy of the production database for testing
A tool that generates code coverage reports
data.e: A mock is a test double that simulates a real dependency, allowing you to set expectations and control outputs.

data.q: In Sinon, how do you create a stub that calls a fake function on the first call and the real function on subsequent calls?
data.e: Sinon's onCall(n) API lets you define behavior per call index; callThrough() delegates to the original method.

data.q: What is the purpose of jest.clearAllMocks()?
o: Removes all mock implementations but keeps the mock functions
Deletes all mock functions from memory
Resets call counts and mock implementations
data.e: clearAllMocks resets mock call info (calls, instances, results) but does not restore original implementations; use restoreAllMocks for that.

data.q: When testing a React component with Jest and React Testing Library, why might you mock a custom hook?
o: To isolate the component from the hook's internal logic and side effects
To increase code coverage of the hook
To test the hook's implementation details
To make the test run slower
data.e: Mocking a custom hook lets you control its return values and avoid side effects (e.g., API calls) in component tests.

data.q: Which statement about 'shallow rendering' vs 'full rendering' in enzyme (or similar) relates to mocking?
o: Shallow rendering automatically mocks all child components
Full rendering requires manual mocking of all dependencies
Shallow rendering avoids rendering children, reducing need to mock their dependencies
Full rendering is faster because it mocks less
data.e: Shallow rendering only renders the component itself, so you don't need to mock child components' dependencies.

data.q: In a test, you want to verify that a callback passed to a function was invoked exactly once with a specific argument. Which Jest assertion is most appropriate?
data.e: Chaining toHaveBeenCalledTimes and toHaveBeenCalledWith ensures both call count and arguments match.
